questions.q: Which statement is the correct definition of a p-value?
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The probability that the result was caused by luck alone in this specific sample
The probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true
questions.explain: A p-value is conditional on the null being true. It is not the probability of either hypothesis.

questions.q: A test returns p = 0.03. Which conclusion is justified?
options: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
If the null were true, data this extreme would turn up about 3% of the time
The effect is 97% likely to be real
The effect is large enough to act on
questions.explain: Only the second statement describes the data given the null. The others misread p as a probability of a hypothesis or as an effect size.

questions.q: You run 5,000 A/A tests (no real difference). Roughly what share of p-values falls below 0.05?
options: About 50%
About 95%
About 5%
Almost none, because there is no effect
questions.explain: Under a true null, p-values are uniform between 0 and 1, so about 5% fall below 0.05. That is what alpha = 0.05 means.

questions.q: With 200,000 customers per group, a 30-cent difference gives p near 1e-15. What should you conclude?
options: The effect is huge
The result is meaningless because p is too small
The null must be true
The difference is statistically detectable, but the effect size is tiny and may not matter to the business
questions.explain: Large samples make even trivial differences significant. Report effect size and judge practical importance separately.

questions.q: Why should alpha be chosen before running the test?
options: So the decision rule isn't adjusted after seeing the p-value to get the answer you want
Because alpha is calculated from the data
Because alpha must always be 0.05
Because a smaller alpha guarantees a true result
questions.explain: Fixing the threshold in advance keeps the false-alarm rate honest. 0.05 is a convention and the right level depends on the cost of errors.
